other_side: Zitron's most recent long piece is about something wider — what he calls the hypernormalised state of the AI industry, borrowing Adam Curtis's phrase for a world where the powerful manage narratives rather than face reality — but it lands squarely on this edition's idea. He argues that commentators rationalise LLMs producing a mediocre-but-plausible attempt at text or code faster than a person as 'impressive', without asking whether impressive translates to useful. His sharper point is aimed at the loop-and-graph culture directly: models tell every user their idea is genius, and are very good at making you feel productive as you endlessly prompt an ever-growing system, creating, in his words, 'the appearance of productivity' without much value. He concedes some people have built automations that help them — 'good for you!' — but says that is nowhere near enough to justify a trillion-plus dollars, and that LLMs have improved in the last year without yielding a product you can describe in a sentence.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether an agent running unattended produces finished work or merely the feeling of it. Both accept as fact that every agentic tool already loops behind the scenes, that coding is where this works because the compiler is a free referee. The empirical question that will resolve is whether knowledge-work loops converge on outputs a manager would accept without rework; the observable is firms publishing before-and-after figures for looped tasks rather than token counts. The pure worldview residue is whether 'designing the referee' is a real skill or a treadmill of tinkering. NLW is vindicated if the April–May agentic flip shows up as measured output, not just spend. Zitron is vindicated if looped work keeps hitting the letter of its finish line while humans quietly redo it. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is where they agree: a loop's finish line and the work being good are different things. Watch for the first independent study of looped knowledge work measuring rework, not tokens.
